newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ bows to pressure, decides against cash rate.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ bows to pressure, decides against cash rate.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand on Thursday bowed to market pressures and turned away from a planned move to change its regulatory lever for monetary policy to an overnight cash rate.

After drawn-out discussions with financial markets opposed to change, the central bank said it would not switch to the cash rate from its present system of using a daily target for settlement cash balances.
The possible changes had been canvassed in a consultative paper released in March, and followed up with direct talks with money and debt market practitioners and economists.

"After reviewing the submissions and in light of consultations, the bank has decided not to proceed with the proposals contained in the consultative paper," Governor Don Brash said in a statement to the markets.
ANZ Treasurer Grant Spencer had said his bank's submission to the Reserve Bank argued in favour of keeping a settlement cash target and rejecting the proposed change to a cash rate.
"We felt it risked generating some instability, particularly in the exchange rate, and that also it risked heightening the Reserve Bank's profile more than was really necessary," he said.
Another economist who declined to be identified said the RBNZ had run into considerable opposition to its plans.
"We got the feeling that the vigour of some of the criticism would have dampened their enthusiasm for going the whole way," he said.

However, the RBNZ said in a parallel statement that it would alter the way in which it assessed monetary conditions in its June 27 Monetary Policy Statement (MPS). Nominal interest rates and the exchange rate would no longer be assumed to be constant in its projections, the bank said.
"Instead the statement will show inflation returning to near the middle of the 0-3 percent target range and a path for how monetary conditions may need to evolve to achieve this."

The bank said the change arose because for the first time it was using a new model of the New Zealand economy to produce projections underlying the statement. "It is important to note that this change in presentation ... does not inherently provide new information about our judgments of the extent of inflation pressures. It simply makes the potential implications for future monetary conditions more explicit."

The bank said it would continue to use a monetary conditions index as a guide to signalling its intentions, with the same 2:1 ratio of a 100 basis point move in the 90-day rate having about the same impact on aggregate demand as a two percent rise or fall in the currency's Trade-Weighted Index. While the announcement had little tangible impact on the financial markets, some forex and bond dealers said a certain amount had been read into the statement.

"They are forecasting an inflation rate to be between zero and three percent, ie 1.5 (percent). If we look at their current forecasts, they are at about 0.8, so therefore it's about 0.7 percent of interest rate movement available to ease from here. That's the speculation," one dealer said. The RBNZ is widely expected to signal a mild easing in monetary policy in its June MPS.
